title: Customer Churn Analysis — Verified Findings Report
executive_summary: Across 749 customers, 37.65% have churned, at an average monthly fee of $42.11. Plan-level churn is nearly flat (Basic 38.87% vs Premium 36.60%), but contract type is decisive: Monthly contracts churn at 48.32% versus 21.85% for Annual, a 121.11% relative increase. A defined at-risk segment of 100 customers (5+ support tickets, satisfaction <=2) churns at 71.0%. Lifetime value scales sharply with plan, from $463.46 (Basic) to $1,816.78 (Premium, +292.01%). Retention efforts should prioritise monthly-contract customers and early intervention with high-ticket, low-satisfaction accounts.

key_findings.statement: The cleaned dataset covers 749 customers, with an overall churn rate of 37.65% and a mean monthly fee of $42.11.
Churn differs little by plan: Basic is highest at 38.87%, followed by Standard (36.68%) and Premium (36.60%) — a gap of only 2.27 points between Basic and Premium.
Cohort churn is broadly stable: 2024 is highest at 39.83%, followed by 2021 (38.02%), 2023 (37.05%) and 2022 (36.74%) — a spread of 3.09 points between the highest and lowest cohorts.
Contract type is the strongest churn differentiator: Monthly contracts churn at 48.32% versus 21.85% for Annual — a 121.11% relative increase, i.e. 26.47 points higher.
The at-risk segment (support_tickets >= 5 and satisfaction_score <= 2) contains 100 customers — 13.35% of the base — and churns at 71.0%, roughly 1.89x the overall churn rate.
Mean tenure is 20.81 months (median 19.0; sample standard deviation 13.25). Mean satisfaction is 3.42, with 27 customers missing a satisfaction score.
Mean lifetime value rises steeply by plan: $463.46 (Basic), $868.83 (Standard) and $1,816.78 (Premium) — Premium is 292.01% higher than Basic.

limitations: Plan-level churn differences are small (about 2.3 points) and were not tested for statistical significance; they may reflect sampling variation.
27 customers have missing satisfaction scores and are excluded from satisfaction-dependent metrics; if missingness is not random, the satisfaction mean and at-risk segment may be biased.
Findings are associational, not causal: the annual-contract advantage may partly reflect self-selection by more committed customers.
Cohort and plan comparisons are unadjusted for confounders (e.g., contract mix within cohorts), and no confidence intervals were produced.
Churn is a snapshot flag; churn timing, seasonality and the revenue impact of churned customers were not analysed.
conclusion: With 37.65% overall churn, the clearest levers are migrating Monthly customers (48.32% churn) to Annual contracts (21.85%) and intervening early with the 100-customer at-risk segment churning at 71.0%. Premium customers deliver $1,816.78 mean LTV, 292.01% above Basic, so retaining and upselling higher-value plans maximises preserved revenue.
